title: Vertical charge-coupled strings store 64 bits per pillar without capacitors
idea: A bit is just a charge packet and needs only a potential well, not a capacitor plus transistor. Use NAND-like vertical pillars whose tiered gates clock 3-phase wells that shift packets to one sense amplifier at the pillar top: 192 tiers give 64 bits per pillar at 60 nm pitch.
why: ~56 nm2/bit (~15x today) with one contact per 64 bits; deletes per-cell capacitor dielectric (Zr/Hf), tungsten contacts and EUV. Transfer inefficiency and serial latency are the risks.
note: Capacitorless vertical CCD shift strings give ~15x density; poly-channel leakage, transfer loss over 64 shifts and serial latency are doubts.

title: Eliminate writability for frozen weights: via-programmed 3D ROM replaces DRAM
idea: Encode a deployed model's weights as present/absent vias in 4-8 stacked metal layers written by maskless e-beam on mature-node wafers, read by low-swing sensing with no refresh or capacitor, with only activations kept in DRAM.
why: Weights are ~50% of inference memory; ROM reads at ~0.05 pJ/bit with zero refresh and frees DRAM supply, using no EUV or high-AR capacitor.
note: Via-programmed ROM for frozen weights; hardwired-model chips exist; e-beam write throughput for big models is a doubt.

title: Via-ROM for frozen AI weights: nothing to refresh
idea: Inverts 'working memory must be rewritable': store fixed model weights as present/absent or size-coded (2-bit) vias in a dense crosspoint read-only array using two custom mask layers on a mature node; changing the model re-spins only the via mask, and only activations use DRAM.
why: Zero refresh power with no capacitor, high-k or tungsten pillars; frees 50-80% of inference DRAM/HBM at 2-4 bits per F2.
note: Hardwired weights proven concept; useful only for frozen models, re-spin cost per model update.

title: Lifetime-leased refresh: streamed and dead data are never refreshed
idea: A lease table in the memory controller (or HBM base die) puts each 2 MB region in one of three classes. (i) 'Dead': freed pages, retired KV. (ii) 'Streamed with period <= P': weights and live KV in LLM decode, read every token. (iii) 'Normal'. Class (ii) rows are restored as a side effect of every full activation. A per-region activation timestamp certifies that each row was opened within tREF, and the controller issues a targeted refresh only for rows that miss the deadline. Class (i) rows get no refresh at all. For most of an inference HBM, the all-bank REF command and its tRFC blackout disappear. A further step is an HBM bin specified for 'access-guaranteed' use, with a relaxed retention screen. Dies that fail today's 32 ms retention test become usable for weights.
why: Refresh energy -> ~0 for streamed and dead regions, and 5-15% more usable HBM bandwidth in bandwidth-bound decode (x1.05-1.18 tokens/s), with no cell change. General servers with 30-50% dead memory get refresh energy x0.5-0.7.

title: Negative-capacitance bitline: electrophysiology's capacitance neutralisation applied to the DRAM sense path
idea: A small amplifier per bitline (or a pre-phase folded into the existing sense amplifier) senses the bitline and drives a feedback capacitor Cf with gain A > 1. That injects a current equal to -Cn*dV/dt, with Cn = (A-1)*Cf. For the 1-2 ns of charge sharing, the bitline's effective capacitance becomes Cbl - Cn; then the neutraliser switches off and the normal latch fires. At Cn/Cbl ~0.7 the cell can shrink 3.3x for the same signal. Amplifier offset is auto-zeroed during precharge.
why: Capacitor height falls from 1.3 um to ~260 nm (Cs 5.4 to 1.1 fF) at Cn/Cbl = 0.7, with the same 512-cell bitline. Cost: ~5-8% more periphery area (one amplifier per bitline) and no change to the array architecture.

title: Compact-then-sleep: compress, pack, partial-array self-refresh
idea: The memory controller (phone SoC or server CXL controller) carries a hardware compaction engine. When it detects idle, it walks live pages, LZ4-compresses them (2-3x is typical for Marvell-class engines), packs them into the lowest segments and updates a remap table. It then issues partial-array self-refresh (PASR) masks that leave the vacated segments unrefreshed. Combined with B4-02's ECC-stretched self-refresh interval (1 s at 85 C, longer when cool). On wake, pages decompress on first touch (us-scale, like a minor fault) or eagerly in the background.
why: Idle refresh power /2-3 from compaction alone, and /32-48 with ECC-stretched self-refresh: a 64 GB RDIMM drops from 0.49 W to 10-15 mW.

title: Compression-funded ECC: compressible rows earn slow refresh for free
idea: On write, the controller compresses each line: exponent Huffman for float tensors, base-delta-immediate or zero-run for integers and pointers. If the result is <=54 B, it appends 70 parity bits (t=7 BCH over GF(2^10)) in the same 64 B slot and sets a mode bit in the existing ECC/metadata side-band. A per-row counter tracks whether every line in the row is in 'strong' mode; strong rows move to a slow refresh bin (RAIDR-style Bloom filter) and weak rows stay at 64 ms. A line that becomes incompressible demotes its row immediately, the safe direction. Reads run the full decode only when the cheap syndrome is nonzero.
why: 8-16x lower refresh energy (0.5-1 s interval) on fully compressible rows at zero capacity overhead. Float tensors compress to ~44 B per line, so this covers most of an AI accelerator's DRAM.

title: Thermal arbitrage: keep the bits away from the GPU's heat
idea: HBM sits millimetres from a ~1 kW GPU at 85-95 C (32 ms refresh above 85 C), and server DIMMs run 50-85 C. In a disaggregated design, capacity DRAM (KV pools, cold weights, CXL expanders) moves onto separately liquid-cooled sleds at 30-40 C, linked by optics (B4-14) or CXL. Refresh is set from on-die temperature and canary readings (B4-02), not the 85 C worst case. The cool margin can be spent three ways: (a) 4-30x longer refresh intervals; (b) multi-level rows (B4-05), whose droop budget is a third of single-level; (c) next-generation dies designed to a 'cool spec' with ~30% shorter capacitors.
why: Retention x3.7-18 from 85 C to 35 C (Arrhenius, Ea 0.25-0.55 eV; x32 by the 2x/10 C rule), so refresh energy and busy time fall 4-18x; or Cs 5.4 -> ~3.8 fF (the sense-limited floor), a ~30% shorter pillar.

title: Defect-budget co-design: 100x pattern-defect tolerance to unlock cheap patterning
idea: Every 128-bit word carries 16 BCH (t=2) check bits instead of 8 SECDED bits, decoded in fast logic-process periphery (bonded or under-array). A small CAM remaps the few residual failing words found at test; mat-level sparing (NAND bad-block style) handles clustered pattern defects (line opens, shorts). Retention-weak cells are remapped too. This turns patterning defectivity from a yield killer into a few percent of area overhead.
why: Random-defect tolerance x100 (p 1e-6 -> 1e-4) for +6.25% extra check bits and ~65 remap words per 16 Gb die.

title: ECC-paid capacitor: let the code, not the capacitor, carry the last 4 sigma
idea: Today's ~50 mV sense budget exists so that every one of ~1.7e10 cells reads correctly at ~7 sigma of sense-amp (SA) offset and coupling noise, with only on-die SEC as backup. Re-centre the array on a raw BER target of 1e-4 per read. A t=8 BCH code (80 check bits per 512 data bits) in the memory controller or HBM/CXL logic base die absorbs the errors; optionally the SA fires two extra comparator thresholds to hand one soft-information bit per cell to a NAND-style soft decoder. With dV_min of 26 mV instead of 50 mV, the ZrO2/TiN pillar storage node can hold ~2.7 fF instead of 5.4 fF on the same 512-cell bitline: ~640 nm tall instead of 1,300 nm. An SA's offset is static, so codewords run along the row (each bit through a different SA), and outlier SAs are fused out at test like today's column repair. The same rule gives a 0.6 fF cell on a 64-cell local bitline in a 3D tier.
why: Capacitor height 2.0x lower (1,300 -> ~640 nm, aspect ratio 62 -> 30) at a 1e-4 raw BER, or 2.5x lower (-> ~525 nm, AR 25) at 1e-3, for +9 to +21 points of check bits (15.6-27.3% vs DDR5's 6.25%). 3D or local-bitline tiers need only 0.5-0.6 fF instead of 1.2 fF.

title: HBF weight tier with read-disturb-aware 'weight mode'
idea: HBF stacks NAND dies on TSVs behind an HBM-like interface (OCP spec August 2026: 256 GB/die, 512 GB per 16-high stack, ~1.6 TB/s read). Weights are written once per deployment, while KV and activations stay in DRAM. Each decode step reads every weight page, so a page sees 1e5-3e6 reads per day. Read disturb (pass-voltage stress on the unselected wordlines of a block) then forces periodic reclaim, that is, a rewrite. The 'weight mode' has four parts: program weights in pSLC, or TLC with relaxed retention; interleave each tensor across many blocks so read counts stay even; track per-block read counters and relocate before the disturb limit; and keep a second replica on another die to alternate reads when the disturb budget is tight.
why: HBF claims 8-16x HBM capacity at similar cost. In endurance-safe pSLC weight mode it still gives ~3-5x HBM capacity per $, against HBM's ~3x DDR5 wafer cost per bit.

title: Origami memory stack: one thin membrane folded into N layers, wired through the folds [SPECULATIVE]
idea: Build N memory die images side by side as one continuous thin membrane (an oxide-cell array plus 3-4 metal levels, ~1.5-3 um thick) on a glass carrier with a laser-release layer, wiring neighbouring dies together across the gaps with ordinary BEOL lines. Release the membrane and fold it accordion-style into an N-layer stack bonded with thin adhesive, with fold radii of ~150-300 um. Vertical connectivity is the BEOL wiring that runs continuously around each fold, so there are no TSVs, no micro-bumps and no die-to-die alignment. The folded stack lands on a logic base die like HBM.
why: [SPECULATIVE] HBM-like stacks at near-planar wafer cost per bit: stacking tax 3x -> ~1.05-1.1x (fold loss 4.5-8.6%), with 20,000+ vertical wires per fold.
note: Fold-routed BEOL wires replace TSVs and alignment entirely; doubts: dielectric cracking at folds, heat through adhesive, membrane yield.
